RealDolls were the brainchild of cybersex game pioneer Mike Saenz, originally famous for creating the first digital comic book; a Bladerunner-like series called Shatter that was digitally drawn on the Mac and printed with Apple's first laser printer. Saenz went on to create the first sex simulation game called Mac Playmate, followed by Virtual Valerie which built on the introduction of robust multimedia software like Macromedia Director (later to evolve into Adobe Flash) that empowered a new group of artist-programmers to create simple games without any deep coding skills. A new industry in adult computer games was emerging, coinciding with the popularity of Cyberpunk SciFi and the first wave of VR hype catalyzed by magazines like Mondo 2000 and the early Wired. Unfortunately, this would quickly be superseded by the rise in digital video which allowed porn publishers to transfer video archives to computers. Porn producers quickly realized that it was far more economical to get people to screw in front of a video camera than hire artists to draw and animate the same imagery. (truth be told, much of the rise of the home PC was driven by its ability to serve as a discreet medium for porn beyond the comprehension of parents) The interesting exception was Japan where such adult computer games persisted to the present day, largely because of designers' interest in going beyond the sexually mundane. Perhaps anticipating this shift, Saenz took advantage of the brief peak in this wave of hype to recruit investors for a venture that intended to create the first sex robots. The RealDoll was the prototype, at first simply a posable doll but intended to soon incorporate the latest in animatronics technology and AI. But the company proved more hype than substance and never did manage to get beyond simple dolls, largely because they never really sold very well. This was partly because of their very high prices, but also because of their fundamentally cumbersome nature.

Few of us live truly private lives in homes with a lot of spare space. So those considering buying something like a RealDoll (or an eventual sex robot) face a problem akin to your stereotypical serial killer; where do you hide the body? Think about it. Most of us live with someone else. Most of us now rent our housing. Most of us can't maintain our homes alone and have service people of all sorts coming in periodically. We commonly hire people to move our stuff for us when we move. So where do you keep such a large sex toy out of sight? What do you do when you have to move to a new place? What do you do when you have to get it repaired? How do you dispose of it when it's worn out? Thus the RealDoll market was limited mostly to rich men living alone in their own large and relatively secluded homes, along with a few artists and comedians who bought and flaunted them to be edgy. Most sex toys are designed to be discreet, sometimes disguised to look like other things, but most simply small and easily hidden away. The Japanese, always more pragmatic about this sort of thing, developed another solution; rentals. They opened services that rented these dolls out and transported them in discreet custom-designed containers like appliances.

So I doubt there will ever be an explosion in mainstream sex robot ownership and use. Their market will be about the same as the RealDoll market today; those very few people who can live in seclusion with a lot of space. Our culture is too prudish, sexually repressed, and judgemental. Most companion robots will be asexual, toonish, or pet-like--deliberately avoiding sexual associations even though we know, they WILL be there. So I think AR/VR sex companions will be far more common, because they are ideally discreet. But they too are in competition with the much simpler and cheaper to produce VR porn.
